\section{Positive transfer amplitudes and vacuum normalization}

Let \(\Sigma=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), and let \(T\) be an irreducible nonnegative
matrix with principal eigenvalue \(\lambda_0>0\), positive right eigenvector
\(\psi\), and positive left eigenvector \(\varphi\):
\begin{equation}
 T\psi=\lambda_0\psi,
 \qquad
 \varphi^{\mathsf T}T=\lambda_0\varphi^{\mathsf T}.
\end{equation}
Normalize \(\varphi^{\mathsf T}\psi=1\).

\begin{theorem}[Vacuum Doob transform]
The matrix
\begin{equation}
 P_{ij}=\frac{T_{ij}\psi_j}{\lambda_0\psi_i}
\end{equation}
is stochastic.  The probability vector
\begin{equation}
 \pi_i=\varphi_i\psi_i
\end{equation}
is stationary.  If \(T\) is symmetric, then
\(\pi_i=\psi_i^2/\sum_j\psi_j^2\), and \(P\) is reversible with respect to
\(\pi\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The eigenvector equation gives
\(
 \sum_jP_{ij}=(T\psi)_i/(\lambda_0\psi_i)=1.
\)
Moreover,
\[
 \sum_i\pi_iP_{ij}
 =\sum_i\frac{\varphi_iT_{ij}\psi_j}{\lambda_0}
 =\varphi_j\psi_j=\pi_j.
\]
For symmetric \(T\), left and right eigenvectors coincide up to
normalization, and
\(\pi_iP_{ij}=\psi_iT_{ij}\psi_j/\lambda_0=\pi_jP_{ji}\).
\end{proof}

Let \(M_{ij}\in[0,1]\) be a bad-edge mask and define the bad subkernel
\begin{equation}
 Q_{ij}=M_{ij}P_{ij}.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Inverse-amplitude cancellation]
Set \(V_i=c/\psi_i\), with \(c>0\) chosen so that \(\min_iV_i=1\).  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:inverse-cancel}
 \frac{(QV)_i}{V_i}
 =\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\sum_jM_{ij}T_{ij}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 QV\le q_{\mathrm{vac}}V,
 \qquad
 q_{\mathrm{vac}}
 =\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\max_i\sum_jM_{ij}T_{ij}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Substitute the definitions:
\[
 \frac1{V_i}\sum_jM_{ij}
 \frac{T_{ij}\psi_j}{\lambda_0\psi_i}V_j
 =\frac1{V_i}\sum_jM_{ij}
 \frac{T_{ij}\psi_j}{\lambda_0\psi_i}\frac{c}{\psi_j}
 =\frac1{\lambda_0}\sum_jM_{ij}T_{ij}.
\]
\end{proof}

Writing \(I_i=-\log\psi_i\), the forward weight is
\(V_i\propto e^{I_i}\).  It records the cost of visiting a vacuum-suppressed
boundary state.  The inverse orientation is therefore a substantive part of
H1.
